phases: scoped (tier 2): signing in and out, input handling, Settings → You
headline: All twelve of run 2's fixed findings hold. Two new Majors: the answers kept for offline outlive a session ended on another device, so a revoked browser shows the person's settings offline (the lost-phone journey); and the test pinning the concurrent-write fix can't fail. Two Minors still answer 500 to hostile input (a NUL in an email on the sign-in routes, and an `Origin: null`).

findings.title: After “Sign out everywhere” elsewhere, the revoked browser keeps the person’s data and shows it offline
findings.detail: Finding 23's fix keeps the last `me` and Settings answers in `localStorage` (`sen.api.kept`) and forgets them at *Sign out* and *Sign out everywhere* in that browser. When the session ends anywhere else (another device's *Sign out everywhere*, expiry), this browser gets a 401, and `router.tsx`'s handler only forgets the session in memory and navigates. It never calls `forgetKept()`. Opened offline later, the gate lets it in (it can't ask the server), and Settings → You shows the person's payday and switches from the kept answers. This is the lost-phone journey (§17 *Login*, flows `lost-phone`). Today the kept data is email, names, payday and switches, but the mechanism is what later slices will put money through. Forget the kept answers (and the query cache) on every 401, not only on this browser's own sign-out.

findings.title: The test pinning finding 22's fix can't fail: the test pool runs one transaction at a time
findings.detail: `api.test.ts` *makes two identical writes sent at once one change and one audit entry (22)* fires 5 requests with `Promise.all`, but the test's `app_user` pool is `max: 1`, so the transactions run one after another and the race never happens. Probe: `.for('update')` removed from `setYou`: `pnpm test:db` stays 33/33. The same change against a live API (pool of 3) gave a round with 3 audit rows. Raise the test pool (e.g. `max: 5`) so the test can see the race.

findings.title: A NUL in the email still gives a 500 on both sign-in routes
findings.detail: Finding 20's guard is in `readJson`, which the commands use. The send-code route reads its body itself (`c.req.raw.clone().json()`), and Better Auth's sign-in route reads its own. A `\u0000` in `email` reaches Postgres (22021) and comes back 500. Better Auth's is a 500 with an empty body.

findings.title: An `Origin: null` or malformed Origin on a write gives a 500
findings.detail: The new origin guard does `new URL(origin)`, which throws on `null` (sent by browsers from sandboxed frames, `file:` pages and some redirects) and on junk, and the throw becomes a 500. It should be the 403 the guard means.
findings.evidence:
origin null      {"code":"server","message":"Something went wrong on Sen’s side."} [500]
origin garbage   {"code":"server","message":"Something went wrong on Sen’s side."} [500]

findings.title: A send whose mail server doesn’t answer waits 2 minutes before saying so
findings.detail: Sen now awaits Gmail, so an unreachable SMTP host holds the request for nodemailer's 2-minute connect timeout. Sign-in's button stays disabled with no word until the 502 arrives. A wrong app password fails fast; this is only the unreachable case. A shorter `connectionTimeout` (say 15 s) would say so sooner.

findings.title: The send route falls through to Better Auth for a body it can’t read, and no longer checks Origin
findings.detail: When `email` isn't a string of up to 254 characters, the pre-check is skipped and Better Auth's own handler answers. For a 10 000-character address that's `200 {"success":true}` (Better Auth's answer for an unknown user), so the screen would say a code was sent rather than *invitation-only*. And since the route no longer reaches Better Auth for a readable body, Better Auth's Origin check no longer runs on it: a foreign Origin gets 200. Both are reachable by curl anyway; neither sends a code to anyone who wasn't invited.
